title: Aggregation: GROUP BY, FILTER, ROLLUP and GROUPING SETS
goal: By the end you can fold rows into one row per group, choose between WHERE, HAVING and FILTER for a condition, add subtotal rows with ROLLUP and label them with GROUPING(), and spot the join that makes a sum count rows twice.

warmup.q: The course data has 8 merchants, and 6 of them have payments. How many rows does `SELECT merchant_id, count(*) FROM payments GROUP BY merchant_id` return?
options: 8: one per merchant, with 0 for the two without payments
warmup.why: GROUP BY makes one group per distinct key among the rows it is given. The query reads payments, and a merchant without payments has no row to start a group, so you get 6 rows. Nothing in `payments` mentions merchants 6 and 8. To list all 8 with a 0, start from `merchants` and LEFT JOIN `payments`. One row would be right without the GROUP BY.

sections.h: GROUP BY sorts rows into groups and folds each group into one row
sections.body:
Finance wants each merchant's succeeded volume. You could run one query per merchant, `WHERE merchant_id = 1`, then 2, and so on: eight round trips, and you need the list of merchants first. You could fetch every payment into Kotlin and add them up there. With 37 rows that works. With the million payments of the large data set, you ship a million rows to the JVM to compute 2,500 numbers.

The database can do the adding where the data lives. Start with an **aggregate function**: a function that takes many values and returns one. `count(*)` counts rows, `sum(amount_minor)` adds up a column, and `avg`, `min` and `max` do what their names say. Used on its own, an aggregate folds every row the query sees into one row:

```postgresql
course=# SELECT count(*), sum(amount_minor) FROM payments WHERE status = 'succeeded';
 count |  sum
-------+--------
    30 | 720455
(1 row)
```

`GROUP BY merchant_id` changes one thing. Instead of one pile of rows, PostgreSQL makes one pile for each distinct `merchant_id`, called a **group**, and runs each aggregate on each pile separately. Each group becomes one output row. In Kotlin:

```kotlin
payments.filter { it.status == "succeeded" }
    .groupBy { it.merchantId }                               // sort the rows into piles by key
    .map { (id, ps) -> Row(id, ps.size, ps.sumOf { it.amountMinor }) }   // fold each pile
```

That is the picture for this whole lesson: **sort the rows into groups by key, then fold each group into one row.** The stepper below runs it on the ten March payments. Inside, PostgreSQL either sorts the rows by the key or puts each key into a hash table with one entry per group. EXPLAIN calls these GroupAggregate and HashAggregate, and both give the same answer.

The picture explains the rule that trips everyone up at first. After grouping, an output row stands for a whole group, so a column may appear in the SELECT list only if it has one value per group: a grouping key, or an aggregate. `SELECT merchant_id, status, count(*) ... GROUP BY merchant_id` fails, because merchant 2's group holds succeeded and failed rows, and PostgreSQL will not choose a status for you. There is one exception, and lesson 2 of this track set it up: when you group by a table's primary key, you may select any other column of that table, because the key determines it. `GROUP BY m.merchant_id` lets you print `m.name`.

Two more things follow from the picture. A group exists only if at least one row has that key, so merchants 6 and 8, which have no payments, do not appear at all. And aggregates skip NULLs: `sum` and `avg` ignore them, `count(col)` counts the non-NULL values (lesson 1), and `sum` over no rows returns NULL, not 0.

refs.title: PostgreSQL 18: The GROUP BY and HAVING clauses (table expressions)

sections.h: WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after
sections.body:
Risk wants the merchants with more than five succeeded payments. The obvious query fails:

```postgresql
course=# SELECT merchant_id, count(*) FROM payments WHERE count(*) > 5 GROUP BY merchant_id;
ERROR:  aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE
LINE 1: SELECT merchant_id, count(*) FROM payments WHERE count(*) > ...
                                                         ^
```

Lesson 1 of this track gave the logical order of a SELECT: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, the select list, ORDER BY, LIMIT. WHERE is step 2. It looks at one row at a time, before any group exists, so there is nothing to count yet. **HAVING** is the same kind of filter one step later. It looks at the folded rows, one per group, and keeps those for which its condition is true:

```sql
SELECT merchant_id, count(*) AS payments
FROM payments
WHERE status = 'succeeded'      -- rows: before grouping
GROUP BY merchant_id
HAVING count(*) > 5             -- groups: after folding
ORDER BY merchant_id;           -- merchants 1, 4 and 5
```

The last frame of the stepper above was a HAVING. One query can use both, and they do different jobs: WHERE decides which rows go into the piles, and HAVING decides which piles come out. A condition on single rows, like `status = 'succeeded'`, belongs in WHERE. Then PostgreSQL throws those rows away before it spends any work sorting them into groups.

HAVING also explains a small annoyance. It runs before the select list, so an alias defined there does not exist yet: `HAVING volume > 100000` fails with `column "volume" does not exist`. Repeat the aggregate instead: `HAVING sum(amount_minor) > 100000`. ORDER BY may use a select-list alias, as the SQL standard allows. PostgreSQL also accepts one in GROUP BY, which is its own extension, and Oracle added that only recently.

You can group by any expression, not only a column. Monthly totals group by the month a payment falls in. `date_trunc('month', created_at)` returns the first instant of that month, and `to_char(created_at, 'YYYY-MM')` returns the month as text, such as `2026-03`. Both use the session time zone, which is UTC in the course database. That choice moves money between months: a payment at 23:30 on 31 March, New York time, is 03:30 on 1 April in UTC, so a UTC report counts it in April. Pick the business time zone on purpose, and write it into the query with `AT TIME ZONE` when it is not the session's.

try.title: Filter rows, then filter groups
steps: Run the first query and read the error. Which step of the logical order is WHERE?
Run the HAVING version. Predict which merchants pass before you run it.
Run the monthly query. Then change its HAVING to `HAVING volume > 100000` and run it again.

SELECT merchant_id, count(*) AS payments
FROM payments
WHERE status = 'succeeded'
GROUP BY merchant_id
HAVING count(*) > 5
ORDER BY merchant_id;

SELECT to_char(created_at, 'YYYY-MM') AS month, count(*) AS payments, sum(amount_minor) AS volume
FROM payments
WHERE status = 'succeeded'
GROUP BY month

The first query fails with `ERROR:  aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE`. The HAVING version returns merchants 1 (7 payments), 4 (7) and 5 (6). The monthly query keeps three of the six months:

---------+----------+--------

sections.h: FILTER lets each aggregate fold only the rows it names
sections.body:
Risk now wants one row per merchant with the succeeded and failed counts side by side. `GROUP BY merchant_id, status` has the numbers, but tall: one row per merchant and status. The report wants them wide, with one column per status. Turning values from rows into columns is called **pivoting**.

Go back to the fold. Every aggregate in a grouped query reads the rows of its group. Give one aggregate a condition, and it reads only the rows that pass. SQL spells that `FILTER`:

```sql
SELECT merchant_id,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'succeeded') AS succeeded,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed')    AS failed,
       count(*)                                     AS total
FROM payments
GROUP BY merchant_id;
```

Each group is still read once. The three counts look at the same rows and keep different ones, the way `ps.count { it.status == "failed" }` sits next to `ps.size` in Kotlin. PostgreSQL added FILTER in version 9.4. Before that, and in databases without it, people write `sum(CASE WHEN status = 'failed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`, which gives the same numbers.

FILTER and WHERE are different tools. WHERE removes rows from every aggregate, and a group that loses all its rows disappears: `WHERE status = 'failed' GROUP BY merchant_id` returns only merchants 2, 4 and 7. FILTER removes rows from one aggregate and keeps the group, so a merchant with no failures stays in the report with a 0.

Ratios bring two traps. `count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') * 100 / count(*)` is integer arithmetic in PostgreSQL, as it is in Kotlin: one failure in eight payments gives 12, not 12.5. Write `100.0 *` to make it numeric. And a merchant with no payments makes the denominator 0, which raises `division by zero`. `nullif(x, 0)` returns NULL when x is 0, and dividing by NULL gives NULL, which is the honest answer for "no payments".

The lab combines FILTER with lesson 3's LEFT JOIN, so that merchants with no payments get a row too. For such a merchant the join produces one row padded with NULLs. `count(*)` counts that row and says 1. Count a column from the right table, `count(p.payment_id)`, and you get 0, because the padded row has NULL there.

sections.h: ROLLUP and GROUPING SETS add subtotal rows
sections.body:
Finance wants volume per merchant, a subtotal per country, and a grand total, in one result. With what you have so far, that is three queries glued together:

```sql
SELECT m.country_code, m.name, sum(p.amount_minor) FROM ... GROUP BY m.country_code, m.name
UNION ALL
SELECT m.country_code, NULL,   sum(p.amount_minor) FROM ... GROUP BY m.country_code
UNION ALL
SELECT NULL,           NULL,   sum(p.amount_minor) FROM ...;
```

`UNION ALL` stacks the rows of queries that have the same columns. It works, but you write the FROM and WHERE three times, and PostgreSQL reads the payments three times. Look at what differs between the three parts: only the grouping key. SQL calls each way of grouping a **grouping set**, and lets you list several in one GROUP BY:

```sql
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((m.country_code, m.name), (m.country_code), ())
```

`()` is the empty grouping set: one group that holds every row, which is the grand total. In the picture from the first section, PostgreSQL sorts the same input rows into groups once for each set and folds every group. A hierarchy like this one, where each set drops the last key of the set before, is so common that it has a shorthand: `ROLLUP (m.country_code, m.name)`. Its sibling `CUBE (a, b)` produces every combination, `(a, b)`, `(a)`, `(b)` and `()`, for totals across and down a grid. Both arrived in PostgreSQL 9.5. The stepper shows ROLLUP adding its rows.

In a subtotal row, a column that is not part of that set's key prints as NULL. That causes a real bug. If a key column can itself be NULL, for example a payment that arrived without a channel, its ordinary group shows NULL too, and the two rows look the same. `coalesce(channel, 'all')` labels both of them 'all'. The function **GROUPING(col)** answers the real question: it returns 1 when `col` was rolled up in this row, and 0 when the row has a real value there, NULL included:

```sql
SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(m.name) = 1 THEN 'all merchants' ELSE m.name END AS merchant, ...
```

Sort with it as well. `ORDER BY GROUPING(m.country_code), m.country_code, GROUPING(m.name), m.name` puts each subtotal after its own rows and the grand total last, whatever the labels say.

try.title: Subtotals with ROLLUP
steps: Type `\pset null '∅'` so NULLs are visible. Run the first query and find the four subtotal rows and the grand total.
Run the labelled version. Read the `g` column: what do 0, 1 and 3 mean?
Run the CUBE query. Predict the row count first: 3 statuses and 4 channels.

code.title: psql, database course
code.src:
\pset null '∅'
SELECT m.country_code, m.name, count(*) AS payments, sum(p.amount_minor) AS volume
FROM payments p JOIN merchants m ON m.merchant_id = p.merchant_id
WHERE p.status = 'succeeded'
GROUP BY ROLLUP (m.country_code, m.name)
ORDER BY m.country_code, m.name;

SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(m.country_code) = 1 THEN 'all countries' ELSE m.country_code END AS country,
       CASE WHEN GROUPING(m.name) = 1 THEN 'all merchants' ELSE m.name END AS merchant,
       GROUPING(m.country_code, m.name) AS g,
       sum(p.amount_minor) AS volume
FROM payments p JOIN merchants m ON m.merchant_id = p.merchant_id
WHERE p.status = 'succeeded'
GROUP BY ROLLUP (m.country_code, m.name)
ORDER BY GROUPING(m.country_code), m.country_code, GROUPING(m.name), m.name;

SELECT status, metadata->>'channel' AS channel, count(*)
FROM payments
GROUP BY CUBE (status, metadata->>'channel')
ORDER BY 1, 2;

sections.h: Joining before you aggregate counts rows twice
sections.body:
Lesson 3 ended with a warning, and here it is in full. Show each merchant's payments together with their refunds:

```postgresql
course=# SELECT p.merchant_id, count(*) AS rows, sum(p.amount_minor) AS paid, sum(r.amount_minor) AS refunded
course-# FROM payments p
course-# LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.payment_id = p.payment_id
course-# WHERE p.status = 'succeeded'
course-# GROUP BY p.merchant_id ORDER BY p.merchant_id;
 merchant_id | rows |  paid  | refunded
-------------+------+--------+----------
           1 |    7 |  32934 |     3880
           2 |    3 |   5805 |        ∅
           3 |    4 |   1375 |        ∅
           4 |    7 | 340346 |   173899
           5 |    7 | 383500 |    18000
           7 |    3 |   4495 |        ∅
(6 rows)
```

Harbor Hotel (5) took six payments worth 335,500, yet the query says 383,500 from seven rows. FROM is step 1, so the join ran before the grouping. Payment 5 has two refunds, so the join emitted payment 5 twice, once next to each refund, and its 48,000 went into the group twice. GROUP BY folds whatever rows it is given. It cannot know that two of them are the same payment. There is no error, and five of the six merchants come out right, which is how this bug survives code review.

The rule: **a join to a one-to-many child repeats the parent once per child, so fold each child down to one row per key before you join it.** A query in parentheses in FROM, with an alias, acts like a table (lesson 5 covers these subqueries properly):

```sql
SELECT p.merchant_id, sum(p.amount_minor) AS paid, coalesce(sum(r.refunded), 0) AS refunded
FROM payments p
LEFT JOIN (SELECT payment_id, sum(amount_minor) AS refunded
           FROM refunds
           GROUP BY payment_id) r ON r.payment_id = p.payment_id
WHERE p.status = 'succeeded'
GROUP BY p.merchant_id;
```

The inner query returns at most one row per payment, so the join can no longer repeat a payment, and Harbor Hotel comes out at 335,500.

The tempting shortcut is `sum(DISTINCT p.amount_minor)`, which adds each distinct amount once. It fixes Harbor Hotel by luck and breaks two other merchants. Metro Transit's rides cost 275, 275, 275 and 550, so the distinct sum is 825 instead of 1,375, and Volt Electronics loses two of its three 18,999 payments. DISTINCT works on values, and two real payments can have the same value. To count, `count(DISTINCT p.payment_id)` is safe, because the key is unique. Sums need the pre-aggregation.

try.title: Count a payment twice, then stop
steps: Run the first query. It is the one from the section, plus `sum(DISTINCT ...)`. Compare `paid` and `paid_distinct` for merchants 3, 4 and 5.
Run the second query, which folds the refunds first. Which merchant's `payments` count changed from the first query's row count?

code.title: psql, database course
code.src:
SELECT p.merchant_id, count(*) AS rows,
       sum(p.amount_minor) AS paid, sum(DISTINCT p.amount_minor) AS paid_distinct
FROM payments p
LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.payment_id = p.payment_id
WHERE p.status = 'succeeded'
GROUP BY p.merchant_id
ORDER BY p.merchant_id;

SELECT p.merchant_id, count(*) AS payments, sum(p.amount_minor) AS paid,
       coalesce(sum(r.refunded), 0) AS refunded
FROM payments p
LEFT JOIN (SELECT payment_id, sum(amount_minor) AS refunded
           FROM refunds GROUP BY payment_id) r ON r.payment_id = p.payment_id
WHERE p.status = 'succeeded'
GROUP BY p.merchant_id
ORDER BY p.merchant_id;

try.expect:
The first query shows the two wrong answers next to each other: merchant 5 has `paid` 383500 (payment 5 counted twice) and `paid_distinct` 335500 (right by luck), merchant 3 has 1375 and 825, and merchant 4 has 340346 and 302348. The second query is right for every merchant:

```postgresql
 merchant_id | payments |  paid  | refunded
-------------+----------+--------+----------
           1 |        7 |  32934 |     3880
           2 |        3 |   5805 |        0
           3 |        4 |   1375 |        0
           4 |        7 | 340346 |   173899
           5 |        6 | 335500 |    18000
           7 |        3 |   4495 |        0
(6 rows)
```

Merchant 5 now has 6 rows instead of 7: one row per payment, as GROUP BY needs.

analogy: Think of a clerk closing the day with a box of receipts. GROUP BY is sorting them into one envelope per merchant and writing the count and the total on each envelope. WHERE is throwing out the voided receipts before sorting. HAVING is setting aside the envelopes whose total is too small to report. FILTER is a second line on each envelope that counts only the declined receipts. ROLLUP is putting the envelopes into one box per country, writing a total on each box, and a grand total on the pile of boxes. The analogy breaks at the join trap: a clerk handed two photocopies of one receipt would notice. GROUP BY never notices, because it folds whatever rows the join gives it.
in_your_world: Settlement batches, merchant statements and the monthly fee invoice are all GROUP BY queries, usually with subtotals, and in Oracle reporting code you will meet `GROUP BY ROLLUP`, `GROUPING_ID` and `PIVOT`. JPQL in a Quarkus or Spring repository supports GROUP BY and HAVING too: `select p.merchant.id, count(p), sum(p.amountMinor) from Payment p group by p.merchant.id`. The fan-out bug arrives the day someone adds `left join p.refunds r` to show refund totals in the same query. When a Kafka consumer keeps running per-merchant totals, the same reasoning applies to the events: a redelivered event is a second copy of one payment, and only a key (the idempotency key) can tell it apart. And when you are tempted to pull rows into Kotlin and `groupBy` there, remember that the database returns one row per group instead of every row.
mistake: The most common aggregation bug is summing across two one-to-many joins: payments with refunds, orders with lines and shipments, accounts with cards and payments. Each child repeats its parent, the sums inflate for exactly the rows that have more than one child, and the totals for everyone else stay right, so small tests pass. People make it because the join reads like "attach the refunds", and because `sum(DISTINCT ...)` or `SELECT DISTINCT` makes the symptom vanish on the test data. The fix is to aggregate each child table to one row per join key in a subquery first, then join those results, or to stack the facts with UNION ALL and group once (the worked example). If you see DISTINCT in a reporting query, ask which duplicate it hides.

compare.title: Statuses as columns: Oracle PIVOT and PostgreSQL FILTER

a.label: Oracle
a.title: Oracle (11g and later)
a.src:
-- PIVOT groups by every input column it does not use
SELECT *
FROM (SELECT merchant_id, status, payment_id FROM payments)
PIVOT (count(payment_id) FOR status IN ('succeeded' AS succeeded,
                                        'failed'    AS failed,
                                        'pending'   AS pending))
ORDER BY merchant_id;

-- portable form, in older code everywhere:
--   sum(CASE WHEN status = 'failed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

b.label: PostgreSQL 18
b.title: PostgreSQL 18
b.src:
-- no PIVOT: one FILTER per output column
SELECT merchant_id,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'succeeded') AS succeeded,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed')    AS failed,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'pending')   AS pending
FROM payments
GROUP BY merchant_id
ORDER BY merchant_id;

-- the tablefunc extension's crosstab() also pivots,
-- but FILTER is plain SQL and easier to read

compare.note: Both queries return one row per merchant with a column per status. Oracle's `PIVOT` groups implicitly by every column of its input that is neither aggregated nor pivoted, so an extra column in the inner query (say `created_at`) silently turns the result into one row per payment. That is why the input is a narrow subquery. PostgreSQL has no PIVOT; FILTER makes the grouping explicit in GROUP BY. Oracle's newest release, AI Database 26ai, also accepts the standard `FILTER` clause and a GROUP BY that uses select-list aliases, so the PostgreSQL form ports there. `ROLLUP`, `CUBE`, `GROUPING SETS` and `GROUPING()` are the same in both. Oracle's `GROUPING_ID(a, b)` does what PostgreSQL's `GROUPING(a, b)` does with several arguments.

worked.title: A monthly statement for Volt Electronics, without counting anything twice

steps.say: Volt Electronics (merchant 4) wants a statement: per month, the succeeded payments it took, the refunds it gave, and the net, plus a total line. Refunds count in the month they were issued. Joining payments to refunds would pair rows and risk the repeat from the last section, so stack the two kinds of money movement into one list instead. `UNION ALL` puts one query's rows under the other's, and pairs nothing.
steps.code:
-- 1. one row per money movement, tagged with its kind
SELECT to_char(p.created_at, 'YYYY-MM') AS month, 'payment' AS kind, p.amount_minor
FROM payments p
WHERE p.merchant_id = 4 AND p.status = 'succeeded'
UNION ALL
SELECT to_char(r.created_at, 'YYYY-MM'), 'refund', r.amount_minor
FROM refunds r
JOIN payments p ON p.payment_id = r.payment_id   -- one payment per refund: no repeat
WHERE p.merchant_id = 4;
-- 10 rows: 7 payments and 3 refunds

steps.say: Group the movements by month and split the fold with FILTER: one sum for payments, one for refunds. Wrap them in coalesce, because a month with no refunds has a FILTER sum over no rows, which is NULL.
steps.code:
-- 2. fold per month; each sum reads only its own kind
SELECT month,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'payment')                       AS payments,
       coalesce(sum(amount_minor) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'payment'), 0) AS gross,
       coalesce(sum(amount_minor) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'refund'), 0)  AS refunds
FROM ( /* the UNION ALL from step 1 */ ) AS movements
GROUP BY month;

steps.say: Add the total line with `ROLLUP (month)`, which is `GROUPING SETS ((month), ())`. Label it with GROUPING, and sort it last with GROUPING too.
steps.code:
-- 3. the statement
SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(month) = 1 THEN 'total' ELSE month END AS month,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'payment')                         AS payments,
       coalesce(sum(amount_minor) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'payment'), 0)   AS gross,
       coalesce(sum(amount_minor) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'refund'), 0)    AS refunds,
       coalesce(sum(amount_minor) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'payment'), 0)
     - coalesce(sum(amount_minor) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'refund'), 0)    AS net
FROM ( /* the UNION ALL from step 1 */ ) AS movements
GROUP BY ROLLUP (month)
ORDER BY GROUPING(month), month;

steps.say: Check the result against what you already know. The gross total, 340,346, matches Volt's `paid` in the last Try it, and the refunds, 173,899, match its `refunded`. March shows the three 18,999 payments, including the duplicate 18, and the refund of 18 the next day. January nets to 0: payment 3 was refunded in full as fraud.

lab.title: A status pivot, a rollup with honest labels, and a sum that counts once
steps: With Docker running, run the tests from the `labs` folder. All six fail, and each failure prints the rows the test expected next to the rows your query returned.
In `merchant_status_report.sql`, list all 8 merchants with per-status counts and a failure percentage. Use FILTER, and check the two merchants with no payments and merchant 4's 12.5.
In `quarterly_channel_rollup.sql`, add the quarter subtotals and the grand total with ROLLUP. Label the added rows 'all' with GROUPING(), so a payment without a channel keeps a NULL channel.

Run the tests until all six pass. Each exercise has a second test that adds rows first, so a hard-coded answer fails it.
hints: For a merchant with no payments, the LEFT JOIN makes one row of NULLs. `count(*)` counts it; `count(p.payment_id)` does not. `count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.status = 'failed')` is 0 there, because NULL = 'failed' is not true.

Name the two grouping expressions once in a subquery in FROM (`to_char(created_at, 'YYYY-"Q"Q') AS quarter, metadata->>'channel' AS channel`), then `GROUP BY ROLLUP (quarter, channel)` and `ORDER BY GROUPING(quarter), quarter, GROUPING(channel), channel`.

drill.title: Write a grouped report from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write one query over `payments`: per merchant, the number of succeeded payments, their total amount, and the number of failed payments, keeping only merchants with at least one failure, plus a grand total row whose merchant column says 'all'. Then say which clause would be wrong if you used WHERE instead of FILTER for the failed count.

answer.src:
SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(merchant_id) = 1 THEN 'all' ELSE merchant_id::text END AS merchant,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'succeeded')          AS succeeded,
       sum(amount_minor) FILTER (WHERE status = 'succeeded') AS volume,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed')             AS failed
FROM payments
GROUP BY ROLLUP (merchant_id)
HAVING count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') > 0     -- groups, after folding
ORDER BY GROUPING(merchant_id), merchant_id;
-- merchants 2, 4 and 7, then 'all' with 30 succeeded, 720455 and 5 failed.
-- WHERE status = 'failed' would remove the succeeded rows from every aggregate,
-- so succeeded and volume would come out as 0 and NULL.

recap: GROUP BY sorts rows into one group per distinct key and folds each group into one row. Only keys, aggregates and columns determined by a grouped primary key may appear in the SELECT list.
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters the folded groups after. Neither can see a select-list alias.
`agg(...) FILTER (WHERE ...)` folds only some rows of the group, which pivots values into columns in one pass. Watch integer division and divide by `nullif(x, 0)`.
`ROLLUP (a, b)` is `GROUPING SETS ((a, b), (a), ())`; CUBE gives every combination. GROUPING(col) tells a subtotal's NULL from a real NULL.
A join to a one-to-many child repeats the parent per child, so fold each child to one row per key before joining. `sum(DISTINCT ...)` is not a fix.

quiz.q: `SELECT country_code, count(*) FROM merchants WHERE count(*) > 1 GROUP BY country_code` fails. What is the fix?
options: Write `WHERE count > 1` using the column name
quiz.why: WHERE runs on single rows before any group exists, so it cannot use an aggregate. HAVING runs on the folded rows. Adding an aggregate to GROUP BY is not allowed either, and `count` in WHERE is not a column at all.

quiz.q: Merchants 2, 4 and 7 have failed payments; 6 merchants have payments in all. How many rows does `SELECT merchant_id, count(*) FROM payments WHERE status = 'failed' GROUP BY merchant_id` return?
quiz.why: WHERE removes the other rows before grouping, so only merchants 2, 4 and 7 have rows to start a group. To keep all six with a 0, put the condition on the aggregate: `count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed')`.

quiz.q: An order has 3 lines and 2 shipments. A report runs `orders o JOIN order_lines l ON ... JOIN shipments s ON ...` and then `sum(l.quantity)` per order. How many times is each line's quantity added?
options: It depends on the join method PostgreSQL picks
quiz.why: The join pairs every line with every shipment of the same order: 3 x 2 = 6 rows, so each line appears twice. The join method never changes the result. Fold lines and shipments to one row per order each, then join.

quiz.q: A report groups by `ROLLUP (region)` and labels the total row with `coalesce(region, 'Total')`. Some customers have a NULL region. What does the output show?
options: Two rows labelled Total, one of them only the customers with no region
One Total row; ROLLUP merges the NULL group into it
An error: ROLLUP does not allow NULL keys
quiz.why: The NULL-region customers form an ordinary group whose key is NULL, and the grand total row also has NULL there. coalesce cannot tell them apart. `CASE WHEN GROUPING(region) = 1 THEN 'Total' ELSE region END` can: GROUPING is 1 only on the rolled-up row.

quiz.q: `merchants m LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id ... GROUP BY m.merchant_id`. Paper Lantern Books has no payments. What do `count(*)` and `count(p.payment_id)` return for it?
quiz.why: Lesson 3's LEFT JOIN emits one row for an unmatched merchant, with NULL in every payments column. `count(*)` counts rows, so it says 1. `count(p.payment_id)` counts non-NULL values, so it says 0, which is the answer you want.

flashcards.front: What may appear in the SELECT list of a grouped query?
flashcards.back: Grouping keys, aggregates, and columns of a table whose primary key is grouped (they depend on it).

flashcards.front: WHERE or HAVING: which runs first, and on what?
flashcards.back: WHERE, on single rows before grouping. HAVING runs after folding, on one row per group.
Only the rows of the group that pass the condition. Other aggregates in the same query still see every row.

flashcards.front: `ROLLUP (a, b)` is shorthand for which grouping sets?
flashcards.back: `GROUPING SETS ((a, b), (a), ())`. `CUBE (a, b)` adds `(b)` as well.

flashcards.front: How do you tell a subtotal row from a group whose key is NULL?
flashcards.back: `GROUPING(col)` is 1 when col was rolled up in that row and 0 for a real value, NULL included.

flashcards.front: Why does `sum(p.amount)` inflate after joining payments to refunds?
flashcards.back: The join repeats a payment once per refund, and GROUP BY folds every repeat. Fold refunds per payment first.

flashcards.front: What does `sum(x)` return over zero rows?
flashcards.back: NULL, not 0. Wrap it in `coalesce(sum(x), 0)` when 0 is the right answer.

terms.plain: A function that folds many values into one: count, sum, avg, min, max.
All input rows that share the same values of the GROUP BY keys. Each group becomes one output row.
A filter on the folded groups, applied after GROUP BY and before the select list.
`agg(...) FILTER (WHERE cond)`: the aggregate reads only the rows of its group that pass cond.
Turning values that sit in rows (one row per status) into columns (one column per status).
One list of grouping keys. GROUPING SETS runs several of them over the same rows in one query.
Shorthands for grouping sets: ROLLUP drops keys from the right for subtotals; CUBE uses every combination.
Returns 1 for a column that was rolled up in this row, 0 where it holds a real value.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate's monthly revenue report showed higher numbers for some merchants after they added a LEFT JOIN to refunds, so they changed `sum(p.amount_minor)` to `sum(DISTINCT p.amount_minor)`. Now other merchants are too low. Explain both bugs and the fix.
explain_back.answer: The join runs before the grouping and emits a payment once for every refund it has, so a payment with two refunds lands in its merchant's group twice and its amount is added twice. GROUP BY cannot tell that two rows are one payment. `sum(DISTINCT ...)` adds each distinct amount once, so two different payments with the same amount, like three 275 bus rides, collapse into one, and those merchants come out low. DISTINCT works on values, not on identities. The fix is to fold the refunds to one row per payment in a subquery, `SELECT payment_id, sum(amount_minor) FROM refunds GROUP BY payment_id`, and LEFT JOIN that, so each payment appears once. Stacking payments and refunds with UNION ALL and grouping once also works.

deeper.body:
How much does ROLLUP save over the UNION ALL of three GROUP BYs? On the large data set (load it with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course -f /seed/load-big.sql`, then `SET search_path = big, public;`), the ROLLUP plan reads the million payments once and keeps three hash tables at the same time:

```postgresql
course=# EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF)
course-# SELECT status, metadata->>'channel' AS channel, count(*), sum(amount_minor)
course-# FROM payments GROUP BY ROLLUP (status, metadata->>'channel');
                                   QUERY PLAN
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 MixedAggregate (actual time=309.529..309.550 rows=16.00 loops=1)
   Hash Key: status, (metadata ->> 'channel'::text)
   Hash Key: status
   Group Key: ()
   Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 105kB
   Buffers: shared hit=977 read=22841
   ->  Seq Scan on payments (actual time=0.291..129.376 rows=1000478.00 loops=1)
(output trimmed)
 Execution Time: 309.694 ms
```

Each `Hash Key` line is one grouping set, and `Group Key: ()` is the grand total. The UNION ALL version reads the table three times: 71,480 buffers against 23,818. On an Apple-silicon laptop it still finished first, in about 250 ms against 310 ms, because PostgreSQL ran its three branches in parallel workers, and it does not run an aggregation with grouping sets in parallel. So ROLLUP is less I/O and one statement to maintain; whether it is faster depends on how many cores are idle. Your times will differ with the machine.

Aggregates can build things other than numbers. `string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY name)` joins strings, `array_agg(payment_id ORDER BY created_at)` builds an array, and `bool_and(status = 'succeeded')` asks whether every row passed. The `ORDER BY` inside the parentheses orders the values fed to that one aggregate. It is the only way to get a defined order inside `string_agg`, because a group, like a table, has no order.

`count(DISTINCT x)` has to remember every distinct value it has seen in the group, so on large groups it sorts and is much slower than `count(*)`. If you need an exact distinct count often, consider a table that keeps one row per (group, value) pair, so the count becomes a plain `count(*)`.
